lessons.title: The forward pass you actually serve
explanation: Training walks a batch, computes a loss, and pushes adjoints backward so every knob can move. Inference is the other job: a forward pass that emits tokens for a user. The tape, the optimizer, and the gradient buffers can stay on the floor. You are serving a function, not fitting one.

Generate time has costs training can hide. Each new token scores the growing prefix. Memory for past keys and values grows with length. Latency is a token clock, not a throughput of minibatches. A training graph that looked cheap can be expensive the moment you decode one sequence at a time.

Decoding choices — greedy, sample, beam — are inference policy, not a new architecture. They pick among the same next-token distribution. Changing the sampler does not retrain the stack. It changes which continuation you ship.
lessons.example: A decoder trained with teacher forcing never had to emit a hundred tokens in a row under a latency budget. At serve time that hundred-step loop is the product, and the backward pass is gone.
lessons.whyItMatters: Confusing train graphs with serve graphs is how people price a model from a training FLOP slide and then miss the KV memory bill.

quiz.stem: Inference, as this course uses it, is the job of:
quiz.correctAnswer: Serving the forward pass without the backward pass you trained

distractors.text: Keeping the tape live so every user token updates the weights
distractors.rationale: Serve does not fit. The knobs stay put.

distractors.text: Replacing the transformer with a database of facts
distractors.rationale: The stack is still a forward pass.

distractors.text: Reporting training loss as if it were a product metric
distractors.rationale: Train loss is not the serve job.

quiz.correctExplanation: Forward only. No adjoints. That is serve.
objectiveIds: Serve the forward pass without the backward pass you trained

quiz.stem: Which cost often dominates generate time even when it did not dominate training?
quiz.correctAnswer: Memory and latency of scoring a growing prefix token by token

distractors.text: The backward pass through every layer on every user token
distractors.rationale: Serve dropped the backward pass.

distractors.text: Shuffling the training set between epochs
distractors.rationale: Epochs are a train loop.

distractors.text: Computing a full Hessian of the pretrain loss
distractors.rationale: Second-order train work is not the serve bill.

quiz.correctExplanation: Length, cache, and per-token latency show up when you decode.
objectiveIds: Name a cost that exists at generate time that did not dominate training

quiz.stem: A training run that looks cheap on minibatch throughput can still be expensive to serve because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Decode is a sequential token clock with a growing prefix, not a batched train step

distractors.text: Serve must recompute the Hessian of the original loss
distractors.rationale: No Hessian at serve.

distractors.text: Every user request refits the entire stack from random
distractors.rationale: Weights stay; only the forward pass runs.

distractors.text: Teacher forcing is required on every generated token
distractors.rationale: Teacher forcing was a train trick.

quiz.correctExplanation: One sequence, many steps, growing history. That is the serve loop.
objectiveIds: Name a cost that exists at generate time that did not dominate training

lessons.title: How much past the model can see
explanation: A context window is the span of tokens the model is allowed to attend to. Positional encodings and the attention implementation set that span. Past the window, earlier tokens are simply not there. They are not compressed into a secret summary unless you built one.

Cost grows with the span. Naive all-pairs attention is quadratic in length. Memory for keys and values is linear in length times layers times heads. Stretching the window is a systems bet, not a free adjective on a slide.

A document longer than the window falls off the left edge. The model continues from what still fits. If the needed fact was in the dropped prefix, fluency will not restore it. Retrieval and summarization exist because the window is finite.
lessons.example: A 4k-token window cannot hold a 40k-token contract. The last clauses sit in view; the definitions at the top do not, unless you retrieve them or chunk the file.
lessons.whyItMatters: Context-window marketing is a length and a cost. Treat it as either and you will stop asking the model to remember a book it cannot attend to.

quiz.stem: A context window, here, is which of the following limits?
quiz.correctAnswer: How much past the model can attend to, and what that costs

distractors.text: How many parameters the stack is allowed to own
distractors.rationale: Parameter count is not the window.

distractors.text: How many epochs you ran in pretraining
distractors.rationale: Epochs are a train loop.

distractors.text: How many tools the host is willing to call
distractors.rationale: Tools are a later loop around the window.

quiz.correctExplanation: Span of tokens plus the bill for scoring them.
objectiveIds: State how much past the model can attend to, and what that costs

quiz.stem: A needed definition sits 50k tokens back in a 4k window. What falls out?
quiz.correctAnswer: That definition is not in the attended prefix, so fluency cannot restore it

distractors.text: The window secretly stores the whole file as one vector
distractors.rationale: Unless you built a summary, the left edge is gone.

distractors.text: Positional encodings fetch any offset for free
distractors.rationale: Positions name tokens that are present, not dropped ones.

distractors.text: The backward pass will recover the missing clause at serve
distractors.rationale: Serve has no backward pass.

quiz.correctExplanation: Out of window is out of the computation. Retrieve or drop.
objectiveIds: Predict what falls out of a window that is shorter than the document

quiz.stem: Why is stretching a window a systems bet rather than a free upgrade?
quiz.correctAnswer: Attention and KV memory grow with length, so the extra span has a bill

distractors.text: Longer windows delete the need for a positional encoding
distractors.rationale: Longer spans need positions more, not less.

distractors.text: The tokenizer shrinks automatically when the window grows
distractors.rationale: Tokenization is a different map.

distractors.text: Training loss becomes the only remaining cost
distractors.rationale: Serve cost is the point of the bet.

quiz.correctExplanation: Quadratic scores or linear cache — someone pays for the extra tokens.
objectiveIds: State how much past the model can attend to, and what that costs

lessons.title: Remember the prefix, do not rebuild it
explanation: Under a causal mask, keys and values of past tokens do not depend on future tokens. Once a token has been scored, its K and V can be stored. The next query only needs to score against that stored prefix plus the new token. Recomputing the whole prefix every step is waste.
The cache is a table: layer, head, position, key/value vectors. It grows with generated length. That is why long conversations get expensive in memory even when each new token is one small matmul.

Validity is the causal contract. If a future token could change a past key, the cache would be a lie. Autoregressive decode is exactly the case where it is not a lie. Bidirectional encode of a whole document is a different job.
lessons.example: Token 1 writes K1,V1. Token 2 writes K2,V2 and scores Q2 against both. Token 3 does not rebuild K1. It appends.
lessons.whyItMatters: Inference price wars and context-window ads both reduce to how you store and score this table.

quiz.stem: A KV cache exists so that generate time can:
quiz.correctAnswer: Remember past keys and values instead of recomputing the prefix

distractors.text: Store gradients so the user can keep training the stack
distractors.rationale: Serve dropped the backward pass.

distractors.text: Replace attention with a hash table of whole documents
distractors.rationale: The cache is K and V of this prefix, not a corpus index.

distractors.text: Delete the causal mask because history is already known
distractors.rationale: The mask is why the cache is valid.

quiz.correctExplanation: Append K and V. Score the new query. Do not rebuild the past.
objectiveIds: Remember past keys and values so you do not recompute the prefix

quiz.stem: Why does a causal mask make that cache valid while generating?
quiz.correctAnswer: Past keys and values do not depend on future tokens under the mask

distractors.text: Queries never change, so you can freeze the whole stack
distractors.rationale: The new query changes. The past K/V do not.

distractors.text: Softmax is not differentiable at generate time
distractors.rationale: Differentiability is a train concern.

distractors.text: The tokenizer forbids future characters from existing
distractors.rationale: The mask is an attention contract, not a spelling rule.

quiz.correctExplanation: No path from the future into past K/V. Append is legal.
objectiveIds: Explain why a causal mask makes that cache valid while generating

quiz.stem: The cache grows with generated length because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Each new token appends another position of keys and values per layer

distractors.text: Each new token stores a full copy of the training set
distractors.rationale: The cache is this prefix, not the corpus.

distractors.text: The optimizer keeps a momentum slot per generated token
distractors.rationale: No optimizer at serve.

distractors.text: The vocabulary grows by one word every step
distractors.rationale: The vocab is fixed. Positions grow.

quiz.correctExplanation: Length times layers times heads. That table is the bill.
objectiveIds: Remember past keys and values so you do not recompute the prefix

lessons.title: Append, tile, and the memory bill
explanation: Prefill scores the prompt as a batch: every prompt token can write its K and V in one pass. Decode then walks one token at a time, appending. The prefill is bandwidth-heavy and parallel. The decode is latency-heavy and sequential. Mixing those two phases in one mental model is how people misread a benchmark.

Because past K/V are reused, the expensive part of decode is often moving that table, not multiplying a new tiny query. Paged and tiled caches exist to keep the table in a layout the matmul can stream. The algorithm did not change. The layout did.

Multi-request serving shares weights and fights over cache memory. A long conversation can evict another user's prefix. That is a scheduler problem sitting on the same causal contract, not a new attention paper.

Invalidate the cache when the prefix actually changes — an edited prompt, a swapped system message, a bidirectional re-encode. Blind reuse after those edits is a silent correctness bug. The mask made the old table legal for the old prefix only.
lessons.example: A 2k-token prompt prefills once. The next 200 generated tokens each append one column. Editing the system prompt at token 50 requires dropping the table from that point, not pretending K1 is still about the new text.
lessons.whyItMatters: If you cannot see the cache as a legal reuse of causal history, you will treat every long-context demo as magic and every OOM as a surprise.

quiz.stem: How does prefill differ from decode in the life of a KV cache?
quiz.correctAnswer: Prefill writes the prompt's K/V in one parallel pass; decode appends one token at a time

distractors.text: Prefill runs the backward pass; decode runs the forward pass
distractors.rationale: Neither phase trains.

distractors.text: Prefill deletes the cache so decode can start from random keys
distractors.rationale: Prefill fills the cache. Decode uses it.

distractors.text: Decode rebuilds the whole prompt on every token by design
distractors.rationale: That is the waste the cache exists to avoid.

quiz.correctExplanation: One batched write of the prompt, then append-only generate.
objectiveIds: Remember past keys and values so you do not recompute the prefix

quiz.stem: Editing the system prompt in the middle of a cached conversation should:
quiz.correctAnswer: Invalidate stored prefix from the edit; those K/V described different text

distractors.text: Keep the old table, since the causal mask still applies to any text
distractors.rationale: The mask legalizes reuse of the same prefix, not a rewritten one.

distractors.text: Retrain the stack so the new prompt has its own weights
distractors.rationale: This is a cache correctness issue, not a training issue.

distractors.text: Grow the vocabulary so the edit becomes a new token type
distractors.rationale: The vocab is not the cache.

quiz.correctExplanation: Different prefix, different K/V. Reuse would be a lie.
objectiveIds: Explain why a causal mask makes that cache valid while generating

quiz.stem: Paged or tiled KV layouts exist mainly because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Decode is often limited by moving the table, so layout becomes the serve problem

distractors.text: The causal mask is illegal unless keys live in 4KB pages
distractors.rationale: The mask is an attention rule, not a page size.

distractors.text: Training requires a page table for every minibatch example
distractors.rationale: This is a serve layout, not a train rule.

distractors.text: Softmax can only run on paged memory
distractors.rationale: Softmax does not care about your allocator.

quiz.correctExplanation: Stream the table you already legally reused. That is the layout bet.
objectiveIds: Remember past keys and values so you do not recompute the prefix

lessons.title: Look it up, then continue
explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation is a host loop: embed a query, fetch passages, stuff them into the prompt, then let the model continue. The weights are not a database. The index is. If the retrieved text is wrong, a fluent continuation of that text is still wrong.

Embeddings make the lookup cheap. They do not make it true. A near neighbor in embedding space is a similar string, not a certified fact. The model will happily treat a bad neighbor as context because that is what the prompt asked it to condition on.

RAG does not replace the context window. It chooses what to put in the window. A long document still has to be chunked. Citations are a product choice about showing the retrieved span, not a proof the span was used faithfully.
lessons.example: Ask for a refund policy. The host retrieves paragraph 4 of the handbook and prepends it. The model continues from that paragraph. If paragraph 4 was the 2019 policy, the fluent answer is last year's rule.
lessons.whyItMatters: Most 'the model made it up' reports on internal tools are a missed retrieval, not a mysterious new failure mode.

quiz.stem: RAG, in this course, is the move where you:
quiz.correctAnswer: Look something up instead of hoping the weights remember

distractors.text: Fine-tune the stack on every document the night before
distractors.rationale: That is adaptation of weights, not a retrieve-then-condition loop.

distractors.text: Delete the prompt so the model must invent the passage
distractors.rationale: RAG adds retrieved text to the prompt.

distractors.text: Replace attention with a SQL query and skip the transformer
distractors.rationale: The model still continues tokens. The host fetched first.

quiz.correctExplanation: Host fetches. Model conditions. Weights are not the index.
objectiveIds: Look something up instead of hoping the weights remember

quiz.stem: Retrieval returns the wrong paragraph and the model writes a fluent policy from it. What failed?
quiz.correctAnswer: The continuation is fluent over a bad retrieve; fluency is not a fact check

distractors.text: The causal mask must have been turned off
distractors.rationale: The mask is unrelated to a bad neighbor.

distractors.text: The embedding space proved the paragraph was the legal policy
distractors.rationale: Near neighbors are similar strings, not certified rules.

distractors.text: Next-token loss cannot run unless retrieval is exact
distractors.rationale: Loss will happily continue a wrong context.

quiz.correctExplanation: Wrong context in, fluent wrong out. That is the RAG failure.
objectiveIds: Predict a failure when retrieval is wrong but the continuation is fluent

quiz.stem: Why does RAG not remove the need for a context window?
quiz.correctAnswer: Retrieved spans still have to fit in the tokens the model can attend to

distractors.text: The index attends for the model, so the window can be zero
distractors.rationale: The model still attends over the stuffed prompt.

distractors.text: Embeddings store the whole corpus inside one parameter
distractors.rationale: The corpus lives in the index, not in one vector.

distractors.text: Prefill is illegal once a retriever exists
distractors.rationale: Prefill still writes the stuffed prompt into the cache.

quiz.correctExplanation: RAG chooses the window's contents. It does not abolish the window.
objectiveIds: Look something up instead of hoping the weights remember

lessons.title: The host runs the action
explanation: Tool use is a loop around the model. The model emits a structured action — a function name, a query, a click. The host runs that action in the real world, writes the result back into the context, and asks for another continuation. The weights did not fetch the weather. The host did.

A single forward pass that only emits prose is not that loop. It can describe a tool. It cannot have called one unless someone outside the softmax ran the call. Agents are this loop with a stopping rule, not a new layer type.

Failures split. The model can emit a malformed action. The host can run a dangerous action faithfully. The result can be stale. Blame the step that actually broke. 'The agent is smart' hides all three.
lessons.example: The model writes `get_price('XYZ')`. The host hits a market API and pastes `184.2` back. The next continuation uses that number. If the API was down, the model did not 'know' a price. The host had nothing to paste.
lessons.whyItMatters: Safety and reliability live in the host loop. Treating tool use as a personality of the weights will miss the permission you just granted.

quiz.stem: Tool use, here, means you let the model:
quiz.correctAnswer: Call a tool, read the result the host wrote back, and continue

distractors.text: Replace the transformer with the tool so no tokens are emitted
distractors.rationale: The model still continues after the host returns.

distractors.text: Train a new head that is the weather API
distractors.rationale: The API is outside the weights.

distractors.text: Store every possible tool result in the KV cache at init
distractors.rationale: Results arrive after the host runs the call.

quiz.correctExplanation: Emit action, host runs it, result re-enters the prompt.
objectiveIds: Let the model call a tool, read the result, and continue

quiz.stem: How does a tool loop differ from a single forward pass that only emits text?
quiz.correctAnswer: The host runs the action and writes the result back

distractors.text: A lone pass already runs shell commands inside softmax
distractors.rationale: Softmax emits tokens. It does not exec.

distractors.text: The tool loop deletes the causal mask
distractors.rationale: The mask stays. The host is extra.

distractors.text: Fine-tuning is required before any function name can be emitted
distractors.rationale: A prompted schema can be enough to emit a call.

quiz.correctExplanation: Outside the model, something ran. That is the difference.
objectiveIds: Distinguish a tool loop from a single forward pass that only emits text

quiz.stem: The model emits a well-formed delete call and the host runs it. Who did the deletion?
quiz.correctAnswer: The host; the model only emitted an action the host chose to execute

distractors.text: The softmax, because probabilities can unlink files
distractors.rationale: Probabilities are numbers. The host has permissions.

distractors.text: The KV cache, which stores destructive side effects
distractors.rationale: The cache stores K/V, not filesystem actions.

distractors.text: Pretraining, which already deleted the file last year
distractors.rationale: Pretrain did not run your host.

quiz.correctExplanation: Permissions sit on the host. The continuation only asked.
objectiveIds: Let the model call a tool, read the result, and continue

lessons.title: A leaderboard is not the job
explanation: Generative models do not have one number that means 'good'. A leaderboard score is one distribution, one prompt style, one metric. Contamination — the test items leaking into the train crawl — can inflate that number without making the product safer or more useful.

What a benchmark cannot see is the job you actually serve: your documents, your users, your cost of a fluent error. Held-out tasks from that job beat a public ranking. Human review, rubric scores, and unit tests on tool calls are evaluations. A screenshot of a chart is not.

Automatic metrics (exact match, overlap, learned judges) each fail in a known way. Exact match punishes a correct paraphrase. Overlap rewards a copied sentence. A judge model has the same contamination and bias risks as the system under test. Use more than one, and keep a slice a human still reads.
lessons.example: A model tops a public QA board whose questions were on the web in 2023. On your internal refund mail it invents policies. The board did not see your mail. Your mail is the evaluation.
lessons.whyItMatters: Shipping from a leaderboard is how you buy contamination and miss the failure your users will actually hit.

quiz.stem: Evaluating a generative model, here, requires more than:
quiz.correctAnswer: A single leaderboard number on a public suite

distractors.text: A held-out slice from the job you actually serve
distractors.rationale: That slice is the evaluation you want.

distractors.text: A human read of a sample of fluent errors
distractors.rationale: Humans seeing errors is part of eval, not the thing we reject.

distractors.text: A unit test on a tool call the host actually ran
distractors.rationale: That is also a real evaluation.

quiz.correctExplanation: One public number is not the job. Your distribution is.
objectiveIds: Evaluate a generative model with more than a leaderboard number

quiz.stem: Contamination, in this lesson, means which of these leaks?
quiz.correctAnswer: Test items that sat in the train crawl, so the number is partly memorization

distractors.text: A validation split you used only to pick a checkpoint
distractors.rationale: That is ordinary model selection, not a leaked public test.

distractors.text: A KV cache that still holds last week's conversation
distractors.rationale: Cache is serve memory, not a benchmark leak.

distractors.text: A learning rate that was too large in pretrain
distractors.rationale: Step size is not contamination.

quiz.correctExplanation: If the test was in the crawl, the board is not unseen.
objectiveIds: Name contamination and the thing a benchmark cannot see

quiz.stem: A public board cannot see your product job because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Your documents, users, and cost of a fluent error are a different distribution

distractors.text: Leaderboards are illegal once a KV cache exists
distractors.rationale: Caches do not outlaw boards. They just are not the job.

distractors.text: Public questions are always harder than internal mail
distractors.rationale: Harder is not the point. Different is the point.

distractors.text: The tokenizer refuses to encode internal jargon
distractors.rationale: Jargon encodes. The board still never scored it.

quiz.correctExplanation: Different distribution, different errors. Measure that.
objectiveIds: Name contamination and the thing a benchmark cannot see

lessons.title: Fluent is not a diagnosis
explanation: A wrong answer can break for different reasons. Reasoning fails when the steps do not follow. Attribution fails when the span the model cites is not the span it used. Calibration fails when a confident token is not a frequent truth. Incentives fail when the objective rewarded looking helpful more than being checkable.

Those are different repairs. More retrieve for attribution. A verifier or a tool for a calculation. A refusal or an uncertainty mark for calibration. A prompt or a fine-tune that stops rewarding a smile. Calling every miss 'the model is dumb' hides the repair.
Fluency is cheap. Next-token training makes local English easy. A diagnosis has to look past the sentence at which contract broke: the retrieve, the arithmetic, the citation, or the incentive.
lessons.example: A refund bot cites section 4 and applies section 7. The prose is clean. The break is attribution, not vocabulary. Fetching section 4 again will not help if the continuation never used it.
lessons.whyItMatters: You cannot patch a system you have only insulted. Name the break or you will buy the wrong knob.

quiz.stem: Which of these are different breaks, not one vague 'dumb model' event?
quiz.correctAnswer: Reasoning, attribution, calibration, and incentive failures

distractors.text: Learning rate, batch size, and warmup as the only four breaks
distractors.rationale: Those are train knobs, not serve failure kinds.

distractors.text: Prefill, decode, and page size as moral categories
distractors.rationale: Those are serve phases, not diagnoses of a wrong answer.

distractors.text: Greedy, sample, and beam as the four ethical failures
distractors.rationale: Samplers are decode policy, not this taxonomy.

quiz.correctExplanation: Four contracts. Four repairs. Not one insult.
objectiveIds: Name reasoning, attribution, calibration, and incentive failures as different breaks

quiz.stem: A fluent answer cites the right document and still applies the wrong rule. What broke?
quiz.correctAnswer: Attribution: the span it showed is not the span it used

distractors.text: The tokenizer, because fluent words cannot encode rules
distractors.rationale: The words encoded fine. The use was wrong.

distractors.text: The KV cache, which always swaps section numbers
distractors.rationale: Cache reuse is not this diagnosis.

distractors.text: Contamination of a public leaderboard
distractors.rationale: This is a local use error, not a leaked test.

quiz.correctExplanation: Shown span ≠ used span. That is attribution.
objectiveIds: Diagnose a fluent answer that fails for a reason other than 'the model is dumb'

quiz.stem: Why is 'the model is dumb' a bad diagnosis for a fluent miss?
quiz.correctAnswer: It hides whether retrieve, steps, citation, or incentive is the contract that broke

distractors.text: Fluent misses are impossible under a causal mask
distractors.rationale: The mask does not prevent a wrong continuation.

distractors.text: Dumbness is a recognized cognitiveType in this course
distractors.rationale: We do not grade models as people.

distractors.text: Only a larger parameter count can be named as a cause
distractors.rationale: Size is not a diagnosis of this answer.

quiz.correctExplanation: Name the contract. Then pick the repair.
objectiveIds: Diagnose a fluent answer that fails for a reason other than 'the model is dumb'

lessons.title: A confident continuation is not a retrieve
explanation: Hallucination, here, is a fluent continuation that is not a retrieved fact and is not licensed by the context you gave. It is a calibration failure of next-token training: the locally likely sentence is emitted with the same machinery as a copied span. The model is not 'lying' in a human sense. It is continuing.

Next-token loss punishes an unlikely token, not a false proposition. If a confident falsehood is locally likely, the objective is satisfied. Nothing in the loss asks 'did a source say this?' unless you built that ask into retrieve, tools, or a later objective.

Mitigations are systems: retrieve first, cite the span, refuse when the window is empty, or train a preference against ungrounded claims. None of those is a personality transplant. They change the contract the continuation has to meet.
lessons.example: Ask for a case citation that is not in the prompt or the index. The model emits a plausible reporter volume and a holding. The holding reads like law. No such case exists. The loss never saw a reason to stop.
lessons.whyItMatters: If you treat hallucination as a moral failing, you will buy a lecture. If you treat it as ungrounded continuation, you will buy a retrieve or a refusal.

quiz.stem: Hallucination, as this lesson uses it, is:
quiz.correctAnswer: A fluent continuation that is not a retrieved fact

distractors.text: Any token the softmax assigned less than 0.5
distractors.rationale: Low probability is not the definition.

distractors.text: A KV cache that ran out of pages
distractors.rationale: Memory pressure is a serve fault, not this word.

distractors.text: A dropout mask that was left on at serve
distractors.rationale: Dropout is a train regularizer.

quiz.correctExplanation: Fluent, ungrounded. That is the object.
objectiveIds: Treat hallucination as a fluent continuation that is not a retrieved fact

quiz.stem: Why does next-token training not, by itself, punish a confident falsehood?
quiz.correctAnswer: The loss scores local token likelihood, not whether a proposition is sourced

distractors.text: Falsehoods are removed from the vocabulary at init
distractors.rationale: The vocab has no truth bit.

distractors.text: The causal mask blocks any untrue future token
distractors.rationale: The mask blocks future context, not falsehood.

distractors.text: Cross-entropy is only defined on retrieved spans
distractors.rationale: CE runs on whatever target text you trained.

quiz.correctExplanation: Likely token, small loss. Truth was never the number.
objectiveIds: Predict why next-token training does not punish a confident falsehood by itself

quiz.stem: A useful repair for ungrounded continuation is to:
quiz.correctAnswer: Change the contract: retrieve, cite, refuse, or train against unsourced claims

distractors.text: Delete the softmax so no token can be confident
distractors.rationale: You still need a distribution to decode.

distractors.text: Train only on punctuation until facts appear
distractors.rationale: Punctuation is not a grounding contract.

distractors.text: Lengthen the window so falsehoods fall out of cache
distractors.rationale: A longer window can still invent.

quiz.correctExplanation: Give the continuation a source test. That is the repair.
objectiveIds: Treat hallucination as a fluent continuation that is not a retrieved fact

lessons.title: Not every pair of tokens has to meet
explanation: Full self-attention scores every query against every key. That is the honest all-pairs bill. Sparse and linear attention bets skip some pairs: a window, a pattern of strides, a learned router, or a kernel that approximates the softmax mix. The hope is that the skipped pairs were not doing the work.

The bet has a failure mode. If the needed token sits outside the pattern, the head cannot read it. Long-context papers are mostly this trade: pay less than n², risk a miss, measure the miss on the job you care about.

Linear attention changes the algebra so the mix is not a full score matrix. It is still a mix of values. It is not a database. Compare it with full scoring on the span you actually serve, not on a slogan about infinity.
lessons.example: A sliding-window head of 256 tokens cannot see a definition 2k tokens back unless another path — a global token, a retrieve, a second layer with a wider pattern — carries it.
lessons.whyItMatters: Context-window ads that skip the all-pairs bill have made a sparsity bet. Name the pairs you dropped or you are reading a press release.

quiz.stem: A sparse or linear attention bet is the move where you:
quiz.correctAnswer: Skip pairs of tokens that you hope do not need to meet

distractors.text: Score every query against every key, then throw the matrix away
distractors.rationale: That still paid n². Sparse never built those scores.

distractors.text: Replace tokens with a SQL join on the training crawl
distractors.rationale: This is still attention, just fewer pairs.

distractors.text: Freeze the KV cache so no new key can ever be written
distractors.rationale: Cache policy is not a sparsity pattern.

quiz.correctExplanation: Fewer meetings, smaller bill, a risk that a needed pair was skipped.
objectiveIds: Skip pairs of tokens that do not need to meet

quiz.stem: Compared with full all-pairs scoring, a windowed sparse head:
quiz.correctAnswer: Pays less than n² and cannot read a token that sits outside the window

distractors.text: Pays the same n² but with a friendlier name
distractors.rationale: If it paid n² it was not sparse.

distractors.text: Always finds any definition in the document for free
distractors.rationale: Outside the pattern is invisible.

distractors.text: Deletes the need for a causal mask
distractors.rationale: Sparsity and causality are different restrictions.

quiz.correctExplanation: Cheaper mix, smaller receptive field. That is the comparison.
objectiveIds: Compare a sparse or linear attention bet with full all-pairs scoring

quiz.stem: A definition the windowed head cannot see will be available only if:
quiz.correctAnswer: Another path — retrieve, a global token, or a wider pattern — carries it

distractors.text: The softmax invents a key for tokens it did not score
distractors.rationale: Unscored keys do not enter the mix.

distractors.text: You set the learning rate to zero at serve
distractors.rationale: Serve is not fitting.

distractors.text: The tokenizer spells the definition as one character
distractors.rationale: Spelling does not create a skipped pair.

quiz.correctExplanation: If the pair never met, some other path has to carry the fact.
